title: US Strikes Iran for Ninth Straight Night as Brent Oil Tops $90 and Ceasefire Collapses
excerpt: Explosions reported across southern Iran and in Tabriz for the first time, while a third American soldier is confirmed killed and oil prices hit their highest level since June.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • US strikes on Iran continue for the ninth night, targeting multiple regions including Tabriz.
  • A third US soldier has died, raising the total American death toll to 17 since February.
  • Brent crude oil prices surpassed $90 for the first time since June, amid falling shipping traffic.
  • Iran has officially withdrawn from its ceasefire agreement with the US, escalating regional tensions.
  • The US launched strikes on Iran for a ninth consecutive night, targeting military sites in Hormozgan, Khuzestan, Bushehr and — for the first time — the northwestern city of Tabriz.
  • A third US soldier was confirmed killed, bringing the total American death toll since the war began on February 28 to 17, with more than 420 wounded.
  • Brent crude surged past $90 a barrel for the first time since June 11, rising 3% on Monday as Strait of Hormuz shipping traffic dropped sharply.
  • Iran formally withdrew from its June ceasefire agreement with Washington, while Kuwait reported a second day of strikes on a desalination plant it called an attack on civilian infrastructure.

Strikes Spread to Tabriz as US Targets Iranian Coast

The United States launched a fresh wave of airstrikes on Iran late Sunday, marking the ninth straight night of attacks in a conflict that has now stretched nearly five months. US Central Command said the strikes were aimed at "degrading Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial vessels and mariners transiting the Strait of Hormuz."

Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported explosions in the port cities of Mahshahr and Imam Khomeini in southwestern Khuzestan province, as well as near Sirik and Jask in southern Hormozgan province and Khvormuj in Bushehr province. Three explosions were also reported near the northwestern city of Tabriz — the first time it has come under attack since the recent escalation began, according to Al Jazeera's correspondent in Tehran.

"Those great people, those great patriots, were out there fighting that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. Iran has been very, very badly damaged. They've lost everything almost militarily."

— Donald Trump, speaking at Joint Base Andrews on July 19

Third US Soldier Killed as Death Toll Mounts

US Central Command confirmed the death of a third American soldier in recent days. The soldier was killed in northern Iraq on Saturday during a "controlled detonation of unexploded ordnance" from a downed Iranian drone, according to CENTCOM. The military also said "unidentified remains" had been found at the site of a deadly Iranian attack in Jordan on Friday, where two US soldiers died and a third was reported missing in action.

The latest casualties bring the total US service members killed since the war began on February 28 to 17, with more than 420 wounded. Iranian authorities have reported at least 46 killed and more than 400 wounded in recent US strikes alone.

Oil Markets React as Hormuz Shipping Drops

Brent crude futures climbed $2.69, or 3.05%, to $90.79 by late Sunday trading, touching their highest level since June 11. US West Texas Intermediate crude rose 2.65% to $84.68 a barrel. Both benchmarks posted gains of roughly 15% last week — the biggest weekly rises since March and April respectively, according to Reuters.

Strait of Hormuz transits fell sharply, with only four vessels making the passage on Sunday, down from eight the previous day, LSEG data showed. The waterway normally handles about one-fifth of global oil trade. US gasoline prices neared $4 a gallon, with GasBuddy reporting a national average of $3.96 — up 14 cents from a week earlier.

"As things stand, we think oil markets are still too complacent about the potential fallout for inventories, which, unlike at the beginning of the war, are at the tightest of the past five years."

— Amarpreet Singh, Barclays analyst

Ceasefire Collapses, Regional Conflict Widens

Iran on Saturday formally withdrew from its preliminary ceasefire agreement with the United States, which was signed in June and had aimed to halt fighting and pave the way for a longer-term peace deal. Trump had previously declared the ceasefire "over" after Iranian attacks on American forces.

The conflict continued to spread across the region. Kuwait reported confronting "hostile drone threats" and said a desalination plant had been attacked for a second consecutive day, causing a fire, in what it called a direct strike on vital civilian infrastructure. Air raid sirens sounded in Bahrain for a second time on Sunday, while Jordan said it shot down three Iranian missiles. Iran's IRGC said four commercial vessels had attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz via an "unsafe route" with US backing — two abandoned the attempt, while the other two were involved in an "accident."

What Comes Next

The escalation raises fresh questions about whether the conflict is heading toward a protracted Middle East war of the kind Trump campaigned against. The US has moved additional warplanes, including refueling aircraft, to the region, the New York Times reported. Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, vowed that Washington would pay for "seeking to escalate the conflict," according to Reuters. With Brent above $90 and gas prices surging, the economic stakes are mounting for the American public as much as the military ones.
